raw_response:
I am seventy years old, and I have worked my land in Quzhou County since I was a boy. My father taught me how to read this soil, and after fifty years, I do not need a book to tell me what it needs. I have five mu of flat, loamy land, and I know better than to gamble on fancy crops at my age. The only sensible path is the one this land has walked for generations: winter wheat followed by summer maize. I will plant improved Jinmai wheat in October because it stands steady against wind and gives a reliable harvest. I will till the ground with the rotary tiller after the maize stalks are chopped, spread my fertilizers—about eighteen kilograms of nitrogen, seven of phosphorus, and five of potassium per mu—and sow before the cold comes. I will irrigate four times: before winter, at green-up, at jointing, and when the grain is filling. Two sprays for weeds and one more if the aphids arrive. When the wheat comes off in early June, I will plant hybrid maize seed the same day into the stubble without ploughing; there is no time to waste before the summer heat, and no-till keeps the moisture in the ground. The maize will take about fifteen kilograms of nitrogen, five of phosphorus, and four of potassium per mu, with two or three irrigations depending on the July rains, and two sprays to keep the weeds and borers down. I know the young technicians say I use too much fertilizer, but I have tried cutting back, and the yield falls. I cannot afford that risk. My bones ache, so I hire machines for the heavy work, but I still walk every row myself to watch the crops. Wheat and maize have steady prices, the grain station buys them, and the government gives a small wheat subsidy. That is enough for an old man to live on.
